public_rationale: He says rising valuations make AI startups 'impossible' to exit by IPO or acquisition. In 2026, before the post, the clearest case of what he describes was acquired. Cursor, an AI coding startup built on others' models that raised round after round at rising valuations, was bought by SpaceX for $60 billion, about twice its $29.3 billion valuation from November 2025. The deal closed in August. Also in 2026, Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, Stripe agreed to buy OpenRouter for $7.5 billion, and Nvidia struck a $6 billion deal with Poolside. These show acquirers paying high prices for venture-backed AI startups. His wider point that exits are hard for most such firms may hold, but the plain claim that exits are 'impossible' is contradicted.
limitations: If 'impossible' is read as hyperbole for 'very hard for most', a handful of large deals would not settle it. The result depends on reading the word as written.
Several sources are news reports, not filings.
His own post lists some of these deals as inflating exit figures, which suggests he means a general difficulty, not literal impossibility.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: AI startups' high valuations and capital needs push valuations to unsustainable heights that make IPOs or acquisitions impossible, making them a bad deal for VCs.

statement.excerpt: AI startups represent a devil’s deal for venture — by virtue of being buzzy “AI” companies, their valuations are naturally high, and by virtue of their capital-intensive businesses, they require more rounds of venture capital, with each round increasing valuations to unsustainable heights that make their IP-light, EBITDA-negative businesses impossible for either an IPO or potential acquisition.

from_speaker: AI startups represent a devil's deal for venture
capital-intensive businesses ... require more rounds of venture capital
each round increasing valuations to unsustainable heights
make their IP-light, EBITDA-negative businesses impossible for either an IPO or potential acquisition
our_interpretation: The checkable core is the result he names: rising valuations make venture-backed AI startups 'impossible' to exit by IPO or acquisition.

The plain reading of 'impossible' is that such startups cannot, as a rule, find an acquirer or public-market buyer at the valuations their rounds have set. Large exits at or above the last private valuation, during the period he describes, would contradict this.
The period is the present state he describes, taken as 2026 up to the post date (October 20, 2026).
criteria.support_condition: In 2026, venture-backed AI startups that raised round after round at rising valuations generally fail to complete IPOs or acquisitions, or exit only at steep discounts to their last private valuation.
criteria.contradiction_condition: In 2026, large venture-backed AI startups with rising private valuations complete acquisitions or IPOs at or above their last private valuation.

evidence.excerpt: The company secured a funding round this past November at a post-money valuation of $29.3 billion, growing in time with increased adoption of AI coding tools.
evidence.explanation: Cursor is a venture-backed AI startup that built on others' models and raised round after round at rising valuations. SpaceX agreed to buy it for $60 billion, about twice its last private valuation. That is an acquisition at a price above its venture valuation.

evidence.excerpt: AI coding startup Cursor is now officially a part of SpaceX, according to an announcement on the Cursor blog.
evidence.explanation: The Cursor acquisition closed before the post. So a high-valuation AI startup did complete an acquisition.

evidence.excerpt: The chip company closed a similar deal last month, striking a $6 billion structured agreement with Poolside, an open-weight model builder. Also last month, financial infrastructure firm Stripe agreed to acquire open-weight model aggregator OpenRouter for $7.5 billion.
evidence.explanation: Several more multi-billion-dollar acquisitions or structured deals for venture-backed AI startups were made in August 2026, alongside Nvidia's agreed $12.9 billion purchase of Hugging Face. Acquirers for such companies plainly existed.
